references.text: God reveals himself to Jacob with the same title: 'I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac.'
Jacob invokes 'the God of my father Abraham and the God of my father Isaac,' the same patriarchal identification.
God speaks to Jacob and says, 'I am God, the God of your father,' using the same revelation formula.
God repeats his identity as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when he sends Moses to Israel.
God again refers to himself as the God of the fathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Elijah covers his face with his cloak in God's presence, just as Moses hid his face out of fear.
The seraphim cover their faces in God's presence, parallel to Moses who hid his face.
Jesus quotes this verse directly: 'I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob' to prove the resurrection.
Jesus refers to the burning bush and quotes God's words about being the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Jesus points to Moses at the thorn bush where the Lord is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Peter proclaims that 'the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers' has glorified Jesus.
Stephen quotes this verse directly in his speech: 'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.' Moses trembled and dared not look.
God is not ashamed to be called the God of the patriarchs, linked to the promises given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Extends the personal revelation in 3:6 into an eternal covenant title for the entire nation of Israel.
Highlights the dual nature of encountering 'the God of the fathers': a source of holy fear for Moses, but comfort for Isaac.
Links God's identity (3:6) directly to His action of delivering the people from Egypt.
